name: libvips
baseline: ImageMagick 7.1.1 (convert/magick; also GraphicsMagick 1.4, Pillow-SIMD 9.5.0, OpenCV 4.10 in the same table)
workload: Wall-clock time and peak memory of one pipeline on a 10,000 x 10,000 pixel 8-bit RGB uncompressed tiled TIFF: load, crop 100 pixels off every edge, shrink by 10% with bilinear interpolation, sharpen with a 3x3 convolution, save.
claimed_speedup: vips-c 0.57 s and 94.28 MB peak versus ImageMagick convert 4.44 s and 1499.29 MB (page column 'times slower' 7.79), GraphicsMagick gm 2.05 s and 1975.81 MB (3.60), Pillow-SIMD 1.51 s and 1040.11 MB (1.96), OpenCV 4.10 3.15 s and 797.67 MB (5.53), ImageMagick via Python imagick 10.53 s (18.47). The fastest libvips row (ppm input, vips-c) is 0.28 s (0.49).
compiler_and_flags: Driver programs built with plain gcc -Wall against pkg-config vips (see vips.c header comment; no optimisation flag, it only builds the thin driver); libvips 8.18 and all competitors used as packaged for Ubuntu 25.04 (versions in the table), so build flags of the libraries are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04; run 12 Aug 2025; governor set to performance per the vips-bench README; OMP_NUM_THREADS=16 and VIPS_CONCURRENCY=16
stars_or_usage: 11.7k stars; used by sharp (Node.js), Mastodon and Ruby on Rails per the repo page
tradeoffs: Demand-driven, horizontally threaded pipeline streams small regions instead of holding whole images, so memory is far lower but the model is lazy (operations build a graph and run at save time). LGPL licence; large API surface (about 300 operations) with bindings for Python, Ruby, PHP, Go, Rust and others. Command-line vips writes temporary files (the wiki says the CLI generates a huge amount of disc traffic).
caveats: First-party table from the libvips project, own driver (github.com/libvips/vips-bench: benchmark.sh, vips.c, vips.sh; best of 5 runs, 2 s sleeps, peak memory sampled with ps every 10 ms); compiler flags of the compared packages are not stated, so this misses tier A. The wiki itself warns: the test does a lot of file IO and little processing, which flatters libvips; the 16-core machine puts single-threaded Pillow, OpenCV and others lower than they would be on one core (a 1-thread libvips row is 0.77 s, 1.35 on the page's scale); bilinear is a poor-quality kernel; ImageMagick, GraphicsMagick, GEGL, OpenImageIO and others have notes about startup time or an unsuitable front end (oiiotool), and libgd needed a JPEG input. A peer-reviewed paper (Cupitt, Martinez, Fuller, Wolthuizen, 'The libvips image processing library', Electronic Imaging 2025, DOI 10.2352/EI.2025.37.12.HPCI-178, listed in doc/cite.md) presents benchmarks too but its host was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so its numbers were not read; a retier to B is possible if the paper is reached. Memory ratio (derived from page data): ImageMagick convert 1499.29 / 94.28 = about 15.9x more peak memory. The libvips repo wiki also has a second, libvips-only benchmark page (Benchmarks) that compares CPUs, not other libraries.
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-c#Graphics listing 'Image processing library' (listing page not opened); numbers from https://github.com/libvips/libvips/wiki/Speed-and-memory-use (read as raw wiki markdown) and the libvips/vips-bench repo
